# Responsible AI

**AI-generated analysis: human review required.** This output was generated by AI and can be wrong. A qualified human analyst must review it before any action is taken.

This page explains what the verdicts mean, where they go wrong, and how to use them safely.

## Purpose

The sample helps a person triage a suspicious link faster. It gathers evidence about the URL, the page's look and the page's code, and suggests a verdict with a plain-language report. It is a learning sample, not a security product.

## Verdicts are advice, a person decides

- Every verdict is a recommendation: `phishing` (block), `suspicious` (warn), `legitimate` (allow), `error_404` (shown as Error 404: the submitted URL returned HTTP 404, so there was no page to judge; allow, risk 10), `site_down` (shown as Site down: the site could not be reached at all; allow, risk 10) or `unknown` (no usable evidence).
- A person should review the evidence before blocking a site, warning users, or reporting a domain. Do not wire the verdict straight into an automatic block without review.
- In a pre-publish gate, route `action` `warn` and `verdict.page_observed: false` to a person too. A page hidden behind a provider warning the browser could not pass is held at `suspicious` (risk at most 69) by design, because the real page was never seen.
- The report cites each agent's evidence so you can check it. If the evidence does not support the verdict, trust the evidence.

## The disclaimer

The service attaches the bold notice at the top of this page itself, so it does not depend on what the model writes. It appears in:

- The web app, in a banner and on verdict badges.

- Every JSON response has a top-level `disclaimer` field (not `GET /health`).
- The orchestrator report (`verdict.report_markdown`) opens and ends with it as a bold line, added after the output guardrail runs.
- HTML reports show it in a bold banner at the top, beside the verdict and in the footer.
- The CSV export has a `disclaimer` column on every row.

## What confidence means

- `risk_score` (0 to 100) is how risky the orchestrator judges the URL. `confidence` (low, medium, high) is how sure it is, given the evidence it had.
- High confidence means the specialists agreed and their evidence was concrete. It is not a probability, and it is not calibrated against real-world phishing rates.
- Low confidence usually means a specialist failed, the page did not load, or the findings disagreed. Treat a low-confidence verdict as "look at this yourself".

## Known failure modes

| Case                                       | What can happen                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| New or not yet weaponized pages            | A phishing domain with an empty page can look harmless                                      |
| Cloaked pages                              | A page that shows different content to bots, Regions or browsers can hide its real purpose  |
| Block pages and bot checks | A bot check or a browser refusal hides the page (when the browser cannot load it, `code_analyst` may read only its raw HTML, signal `static_html_only`). It lowers confidence and is never counted as phishing evidence, so the verdict rests on what else was seen. Capture is passive: the tool does not solve or wait out bot checks. A Cloudflare phishing or malware warning is a third-party verdict and counts as strong evidence. The browser clicks the warning's own proceed button once, only when Cloudflare has enabled it; when the real page is not reached the verdict is at most Suspicious and `page_observed` is `false` |
| Dead sites | A site that is down gets the Site down answer without analysis. A kit that is offline today can come back, so a Site down verdict says nothing about tomorrow |
| Pages that change per visitor or over time | A second scan can get a different answer                                                    |
| Legitimate sites that look like phishing   | New brands, login pages on third-party hosts, or aggressive marketing copy can be flagged. A copy of a brand's sign-in or landing page with a sign-in, account or wallet action on a host the brand does not own is judged at least Suspicious, risk 50 or more, by design, even a demo or the brand's own preview build: on 2026-10-26 one MetaMask documentation preview with a "Connect MetaMask" button was held this way ([evaluation](evaluation.md#accuracy-rerun-2026-10-26)) |
| Content the model refuses                  | Reported as `blocked_by_guardrail`, which counts as suspicious evidence, not a clean result |
| Non-English pages                          | Copy-based signals are weaker                                                               |
| Similar past scans (episodic memory)       | An earlier verdict on a similar URL can bias the orchestrator; it is labelled as context, not evidence, and shown on the result page |

## Models and where they run

| Role         | Model             | Inference profile                    | Where requests run                             |
| ------------ | ----------------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Orchestrator | Claude Opus 5.5   | `us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5`       | US Regions                                     |
| Specialists  | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | `global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5` | Any commercial Region Amazon Bedrock routes to |

To keep specialist traffic in the US, deploy with `-c specialistModel=` set to a `us.` inference profile available to you. See [configuration.md](configuration.md).

## Guardrails and their limits

- Every submitted URL passes an Amazon Bedrock guardrail (input) in the API or in the CSV splitter.
- The final report passes a guardrail (output) in the worker. It masks a US Social Security number, a card number or an AWS access key ID the report quotes; the rest of the report and the verdict are kept.
- Page content seen by the specialists is not run through a guardrail. It is framed as untrusted data, and a model-level refusal becomes a `blocked_by_guardrail` finding.
- No guardrail result ever drops a scan. Every intervention is listed in `guardrail_events` on the scan so you can see it.

## Appropriate use

- Triage of links reported by users or found in email, chat or tickets.
- Learning how multi-agent systems on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore split and combine work.
- Building a first prototype you then test and harden for your own environment.

## Inappropriate use

- Automatic blocking, takedown requests or legal action based on a verdict alone.
- Scanning URLs you are not allowed to visit, or pages that need someone else's credentials.
- Submitting URLs that contain personal data, tokens or passwords (they are stored with the scan).
- Judging people or organizations rather than URLs.

Because a submitted URL is stored with its scan, anyone who deploys this sample is responsible for meeting the data-protection rules that apply to them (for example GDPR or CCPA) if their users may submit URLs that contain personal data. See the [AWS shared responsibility model](https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/shared-responsibility-model/) and [AWS data privacy](https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-privacy/).

## Report a problem

If you find a wrong verdict, a harmful report, or a way to steer an agent, open an issue with the defanged URL (for example `hxxps://example[.]com`) and the scan's report. For security issues, follow [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md#security-issue-notifications) instead.
